Displace means: to push something out of the place it occupies, so that something else takes over that space or role.

Think of it as a two-part action happening at once — something leaves, and something else fills the gap. Sometimes the "something else" is you. Sometimes it's a new technology. Sometimes it's water. The word works across many situations, but this push-out-and-replace logic is always underneath it.
Meaning 1 — To physically move something from where it belongs

This is the most literal meaning. When you displace something, you shift it away from its natural or original position.

  • A powerful explosion can displace walls and ceilings, throwing them off their foundations.
  • A landslide can displace tons of rock, moving them far from where they originally sat.
  • Even something small: if you nudge a carefully placed decoration off-center, you've displaced it.

The key feeling here is that something has been knocked or moved away from where it should be.
Meaning 2 — To replace or push out (people or things)

This is the most common, everyday use of the word. Here, "displace" doesn't just mean to move something — it means to take over its role or position entirely. One thing gets pushed out; something else occupies its spot.

  • Streaming services displaced DVDs. DVDs no longer hold the position they once did.
  • Calculators displaced the slide rule as the go-to tool for mathematics.
  • In many industries, machines are displacing human workers — the machines are taking jobs that people used to do.

Notice: the old thing doesn't just move — it loses its position to something new. That's the sharp distinction between "displace" and simply "move." Displacement implies a takeover.
Meaning 3 — To force people to leave their homes or homeland

This is a deeply serious and widely used meaning, especially in news and history. When people are displaced, they are forced out of their homes, cities, or countries — usually by war, natural disaster, or persecution. They don't leave by choice.

  • The civil war displaced over two million people, who fled to neighbouring countries.
  • Floods displaced thousands of families from their homes in the valley.

You'll often see the phrase "displaced persons" or "internally displaced people (IDPs)" — these refer to refugees or people who have been forced to leave their homes but haven't necessarily crossed a national border.

The emotional weight of this usage is important: it captures not just physical movement, but the loss of belonging, safety, and rootedness.
Meaning 4 — In science: to push a fluid out of the way

When a solid object is placed in a liquid, it shoves some of that liquid aside to make room for itself. That liquid is said to be displaced.

  • When you drop a stone into a bucket of water, the stone displaces some water — the water level rises because the stone has pushed water out of the space it now occupies.
  • A large ship displaces an enormous amount of seawater. In fact, ships are often described by how much water they displace — a ship that displaces 10,000 tonnes pushes aside 10,000 tonnes of water.

This is the principle behind why things float or sink (Archimedes' principle), and "displace" is the precise scientific word used in that context.
Meaning 5 — In psychology: to redirect emotions onto the wrong target

In psychology, displace has a specific and important meaning. When a person feels a strong emotion — like anger, frustration, or fear — about one thing, but redirects that emotion toward something or someone safer or unrelated, they are displacing that emotion.

  • A manager yells at him unfairly at work. He can't fight back. He comes home and displaces his anger onto his family, snapping at them for small things.
  • A student who is terrified of failing an exam displaces that anxiety into obsessive tidying of her room.

The emotion gets "moved" from its real, original target to a substitute target. It's called displacement in psychology, and it's considered an unconscious defence mechanism — the mind's way of handling emotions it finds too difficult to confront directly.

Since it's a regular verb, this is straightforward:

  • Present: The new factory displaces hundreds of workers.
  • Past: The tsunami displaced coastal communities.
  • Future: Technology will displace many more jobs.
  • Continuous: The war is displacing civilians every day.
  • Past participle: Thousands of families have been displaced.

Whenever you see the noun displacement, it comes directly from this verb — it simply refers to the act or result of displacing.

  • "The displacement of workers by automation is a major policy concern."
  • "The displacement of water by the submarine was calculated precisely."
  • "Emotional displacement is a common psychological response to stress."
A Quick Way to Remember It

Think of "dis-" as meaning away (as in "dismiss" = send away, "discard" = throw away). And "place" is, well, place. So displace = to send away from a place. Something gets removed from where it was — and something else (or nothing) fills the void.

Every single use of this word — physical, social, scientific, psychological — traces back to that one clear idea: something is pushed out of the position it held.
